x: Capt. Webster's tuition should prove of the greatest value to those who care to avail themselves of his knowledge and experience, which goes back for many years, during which he has been acquainted with all the world's best field events exponents.

Captain Webster has the gift for describing a race, and he reproduces in a few words the excitement attached to it. The description on pp. 173 and 174 of the 1924 Oylmpic Games Cross Country Race makes extremely thrilling reading.

Webster, of Birchfield, is “on the ground” in distress but quickly rises and goes on. Footer comes along, now 49th, Syd Warboys, 72nd, Arthur Allum, 87th, “W.G.” 103rd, “E.A.” 110th, Frank 120th, and Bill Rice 185th.
To conclude, the athlete is bound to find much of interest in this well-written book and the majority would surprise themselves if the principles laid down by Capt.

Allen (Highgate H.) and Follows (Achilles Oxford) finished in front of Arthur and in his rear such famous runners as Sutherland and Webster, of Birchfield and International fame, which is sufficient testimony as to the merit of our man's running.

Bailey, of Salford, was leading, followed by Holden (Tipton H.), Evenson (Salford H.), Webster (Birchfield H.), Dodd (Wirrall A.C.), Sutherland (Birchfield H.) and —yes! a Belgrave vest—Penny, seventh.
Howland and numerous others, not forgetting Capt.

More by luck that judgment I was well placed in the seventh position, at the end of the first mile, with Bailey (Salford), Holden (Tipton), Evenson (Salford), Webster (Birchfield), Dodd (Wirral A.C.) and Sutherland (Birchfield) in front of me.

We can safely say that the fifth relay is the most critical one in the whole Brighton Relay and this year we entrusted it to Tom Carter, who soon had an old friend and opponent in Webster on his shoulder.

Incidentally, I have had some recourse to Webster and Hays, but my tables have been modified.
